```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))

set.seed(2026)
pop <- rlnorm(1e6, meanlog = log(25), sdlog = 0.6)   # hourly wages, skewed right
mu  <- mean(pop)
n   <- 50
dol <- function(x) paste0(ifelse(x < 0, "-$", "$"), formatC(abs(x), format = "f", digits = 2))
```

We almost never see a population, only a sample from it. Every average computed from a
sample would have come out differently with a different sample, and statistical inference
is the business of saying how differently.

**The question: when we compute an average from one sample, how much should we trust it,
and how large must a difference be before we call it real?**

Simulation answers both by doing what theory only describes: drawing the sample again and
again. The population here is a million hourly wages, skewed right like real wages, with a
true mean of `r dol(mu)`. @fig-boot builds one confidence interval, the first interactive
chart repeats that a few hundred times to show what "95 percent" means, @fig-null builds a
null distribution for a hypothesis test, and the second interactive chart shows how sample
size decides whether a real effect gets detected.

## A bootstrap interval from one sample

Draw 50 workers. The bootstrap treats that sample as a stand-in for the population: draw 50
from it *with replacement*, compute the mean, and repeat 5,000 times. The spread of those
means estimates how much the sample mean would vary across real samples.

```{r}
#| label: bootstrap
x <- sample(pop, n)
boot_means <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))
ci <- quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-boot
#| fig-cap: "Bootstrap distribution of the mean wage from one sample of 50. Shaded: the middle 95 percent, which is the percentile confidence interval. Dashed: the true population mean."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| echo: false
ggplot(data.frame(m = boot_means), aes(m)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(fill = m >= ci[1] & m <= ci[2]), bins = 60, colour = "white",
                 linewidth = 0.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#0072B2", `FALSE` = "#c6dbef")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = mu, y = Inf, label = "true mean", vjust = 1.5, hjust = -0.1, size = 3.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  labs(x = "mean wage in a bootstrap resample", y = "resamples")
```

The sample mean is `r dol(mean(x))` and the 95 percent interval runs from `r dol(ci[1])` to
`r dol(ci[2])`. It happens to contain the true mean. The question is how often that happens.

## What "95 percent" means

The 95 percent is a property of the procedure, not of any one interval: draw a sample, build
the interval, and the interval contains the truth in about 95 percent of repetitions. Here
is the whole procedure repeated a thousand times:

```{r}
#| label: coverage
covers <- replicate(1000, {
  s <- sample(pop, n)
  b <- rowMeans(matrix(sample(s, n * 1000, replace = TRUE), nrow = 1000))
  q <- quantile(b, c(0.025, 0.975))
  q[1] <= mu & mu <= q[2]
})
```

`r round(100 * mean(covers), 1)` percent of the intervals contain the true mean, a little
short of 95. The chart below runs the same experiment in your browser. Each vertical line is
one sample's interval; orange ones miss. Lower the sample size and the miss rate climbs well
past 5 percent, because with skewed data a small sample rarely includes the few high earners
that pull the mean up, so the bootstrap distribution is too narrow. The promise is only
approximately kept, and only once samples are large.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof n1 = Inputs.range([5, 200], {value: 50, step: 1, label: "sample size"})
viewof level1 = Inputs.range([0.80, 0.99], {value: 0.95, step: 0.01, label: "confidence level"})
viewof reps1 = Inputs.range([50, 400], {value: 200, step: 50, label: "repeated samples"})
viewof seed1 = Inputs.button("draw new samples", {value: 1, reduce: v => v + 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
TRUE_MEAN = 25 * Math.exp(0.6 ** 2 / 2)

intervals = {
  const rng = d3.randomLcg(seed1 * 7919 + 13);
  const draw = d3.randomLogNormal.source(rng)(Math.log(25), 0.6);
  const B = 400, a = (1 - level1) / 2;
  const s = new Float64Array(n1), bm = new Float64Array(B), out = [];
  for (let r = 0; r < reps1; r++) {
    let sum = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < n1; i++) { s[i] = draw(); sum += s[i]; }
    for (let b = 0; b < B; b++) {
      let t = 0;
      for (let i = 0; i < n1; i++) t += s[Math.floor(rng() * n1)];
      bm[b] = t / n1;
    }
    bm.sort();
    const lo = d3.quantileSorted(bm, a), hi = d3.quantileSorted(bm, 1 - a);
    out.push({sample: r + 1, mean: sum / n1, lo, hi,
              result: lo <= TRUE_MEAN && TRUE_MEAN <= hi ? "contains the true mean" : "misses"});
  }
  return out;
}

hits1 = intervals.filter(d => d.result !== "misses").length

md`**${hits1} of ${reps1}** intervals (${(100 * hits1 / reps1).toFixed(1)} percent) contain the true mean, against a promised ${Math.round(100 * level1)} percent.`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  height: 320, marginLeft: 50,
  x: {label: "sample", ticks: []},
  y: {label: "hourly wage ($)", domain: [10, 60]},
  color: {domain: ["contains the true mean", "misses"], range: ["#9ecae1", "#D55E00"], legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(intervals, {x: "sample", y1: "lo", y2: "hi", stroke: "result",
                           strokeWidth: reps1 > 250 ? 1 : 2}),
    Plot.ruleY([TRUE_MEAN], {strokeDasharray: "4,3"})
  ]
})
```

## A hypothesis test from a null distribution

Now a policy question. A job-training program is tested on 50 workers, compared with 50
who did not take it. In this simulation the program genuinely raises wages by \$2 an hour.
The null hypothesis is that it does nothing.

If the null were true, both groups would be drawn from the same population, so we can
simulate exactly what the difference in means looks like when nothing is going on, 10,000
times. (With real data, where the population is unknown, shuffling the treatment labels
builds the same distribution from the sample alone.)

```{r}
#| label: test
control  <- sample(pop, n)
treated  <- sample(pop, n) + 2
observed <- mean(treated) - mean(control)

null_diffs <- replicate(10000, mean(sample(pop, n)) - mean(sample(pop, n)))
crit    <- quantile(null_diffs, c(0.025, 0.975))
p_value <- mean(abs(null_diffs) >= abs(observed))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-null
#| fig-cap: "Simulated distribution of the difference in mean wages when the program has no effect. Red: the 5 percent rejection region. Blue lines: the observed difference and its mirror image; the share of the distribution beyond them is the p-value."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| echo: false
ggplot(data.frame(d = null_diffs), aes(d)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(fill = d <= crit[1] | d >= crit[2]), bins = 70, colour = "white",
                 linewidth = 0.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#D55E00", `FALSE` = "grey75")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1) * abs(observed), colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  labs(x = "difference in mean wage, treated minus control", y = "simulated experiments")
```

The rejection region is everything beyond `r dol(crit[1])` and `r dol(crit[2])`: differences
that would arise less than 5 percent of the time if the program did nothing. The observed
difference is `r dol(observed)`. A difference at least that large, in either direction,
shows up in `r round(100 * p_value)` percent of no-effect experiments, so the p-value is
`r formatC(p_value, format = "f", digits = 2)` and the test does not reject.

That is the right reading of a p-value: how surprising the data would be if the null were
true. It is not the probability that the null is true, and here the null is in fact false.
The test simply has too little data to see a \$2 effect against wages this dispersed.

## How much data a real effect needs

Change the true effect, the sample size per group, or the significance level. The grey bars
are the null distribution, the red lines its rejection boundaries, the blue outline 1,000
studies run with the true effect, and the black line the one study drawn this time.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof effect = Inputs.range([0, 8], {value: 2, step: 0.5, label: "true effect ($/hour)"})
viewof n2 = Inputs.range([10, 2000], {value: 50, step: 10, label: "workers per group"})
viewof alpha = Inputs.radio([0.01, 0.05, 0.10], {value: 0.05, label: "significance level"})
viewof seed2 = Inputs.button("run a new study", {value: 1, reduce: v => v + 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
test = {
  const rng = d3.randomLcg(seed2 * 104729 + 7);
  const draw = d3.randomLogNormal.source(rng)(Math.log(25), 0.6);
  const meanOf = (k, shift) => { let t = 0; for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) t += draw(); return t / k + shift; };
  const nullD = Float64Array.from({length: 2000}, () => meanOf(n2, 0) - meanOf(n2, 0)).sort();
  const lo = d3.quantileSorted(nullD, alpha / 2), hi = d3.quantileSorted(nullD, 1 - alpha / 2);
  const altD = Array.from({length: 1000}, () => meanOf(n2, effect) - meanOf(n2, 0));
  const obs = meanOf(n2, effect) - meanOf(n2, 0);
  const p = nullD.filter(d => Math.abs(d) >= Math.abs(obs)).length / nullD.length;
  const power = altD.filter(d => d <= lo || d >= hi).length / altD.length;
  return {nullD: Array.from(nullD), altD, lo, hi, obs, p, power};
}

md`This study: difference **${test.obs < 0 ? "−" : ""}$${Math.abs(test.obs).toFixed(2)}**, p-value **${test.p < 0.001 ? "below 0.001" : test.p.toFixed(3)}**, so the test ${test.p < alpha ? "**rejects**" : "does **not** reject"} at ${alpha}. Across 1,000 studies with a true effect of $${effect.toFixed(1)}, it rejects **${Math.round(100 * test.power)} percent** of the time${effect === 0 ? ", which is the false-positive rate and should be close to " + alpha : ", which is the test's power"}.`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
bins = {
  const ext = d3.extent([...test.nullD, ...test.altD, test.obs]);
  return {domain: ext, thresholds: d3.ticks(ext[0], ext[1], 45)};
}

Plot.plot({
  height: 300, marginLeft: 50,
  x: {label: "difference in mean wage, treated minus control ($)", domain: bins.domain},
  y: {label: "share of studies", tickFormat: "%"},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(test.nullD, Plot.binX({y: "proportion"},
      {x: d => d, fill: "#bdbdbd", thresholds: bins.thresholds, domain: bins.domain})),
    Plot.lineY(test.altD, Plot.binX({y: "proportion"},
      {x: d => d, stroke: "#0072B2", strokeWidth: 2, curve: "step",
       thresholds: bins.thresholds, domain: bins.domain})),
    Plot.ruleX([test.lo, test.hi], {stroke: "#D55E00", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleX([test.obs], {stroke: "black", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})
```

With the true \$2 effect, power is under 10 percent at 50 workers per group. Push the
sample size to about 1,500 and it reaches roughly 80 percent; set the effect to zero and the
test rejects about as often as the significance level, which is what the level means.

## What the four charts show together

@fig-boot and the first interactive chart are two views of one idea: an interval describes
how much an estimate moves from sample to sample, and its "95 percent" is a long-run hit
rate that small samples from skewed populations fall short of. @fig-null and the second
chart apply the same idea to testing: the null distribution shows how much a difference
moves when nothing is going on, the rejection region and p-value are read off it, and
whether a real effect clears that bar depends mostly on how much data there is. In both
cases the quantity that matters is the spread of an estimate across hypothetical samples,
and simulation makes that spread something you can see.
